overview.body:
**Hoderi** ​(*hoderi*) — ‌Fire, Fisherman ‌· ​Fire-shining — ​belongs ​to the ​Japanese tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Fire, ​Fisherman". ‌The name ​means ‌"Fire-shining"[^1].

**Hoderi** ​is the ​elder ​son of ​the ​heavenly grandson ‌Ninigi and ​the ‌blossom princess ​Konohana-Sakuya-hime. ‌His name ​means 'Fire-Shining,' ‌and ​he was ‌gifted ​with the ​fishhook that ‌made ‌him master ‌of ​the sea. ​His story ‌turns ​on the ​rivalry ‌with his ​younger brother ​Hoori, ‌a conflict ​that ‌costs him ​his birthright ​and ​sets the ​imperial ‌line on ‌a new ​path.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the ​name as ‌**Hoderi** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/hoderi/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a ‌description computed ​from the ​displayed ​form itself. ‌The ​plain ASCII ​form *hoderi* ​survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Japanese ​characters ​as ​**火照命**. ​Etymologically ‌it means ​"Fire-shining"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*hoderi* ​survives ‌only because ​the ​early ​domain-name ​system ​could ‌not carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a ​technological ‌compromise, not ​an ‌ancient ​spelling. ​The ‌Unicode ‌restoration ‌**Hoderi** recovers ​the ​full ‌diacritic ​detail ​of ‌the scholarly ​transliteration ​directly ‌in ​the ‌address ​bar. The ​restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— ‌a ​description computed ‌from ​the ​displayed ‌form ‌itself.

‌The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**h** ​→ ​**H** ​— ‌Same, capitalized
- ​**o** ​→ ​**o** ‌— ​Same
- ​**d** → ​**d** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**e** ​→ ‌**e** ​— Same
- ‌**r** ‌→ ​**r** ​— ​Same
- ​**i** → ‌**i** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/ho.de.ɾi/** ​— ​Modern Standard ​Japanese ‌(Hepburn).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Ho-** ​— Voiceless ‌glottal ​[h] ‌plus open-mid ​back ​[o]; ​from 火 ​'fire'
- ​**-de-** ‌— Voiced ​alveolar ‌stop ​[d] plus ‌close-mid ​[e]
- ‌**-ri** — ​Alveolar ‌tap ​[ɾ] plus ​close ‌front ‌[i]; from ‌照 ​'shining'

​For the ‌modern ​speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation ​is: ​'HOH-deh-ree' — ‌the ​'r' is ‌a ​light ​tap, and ​all ​vowels ‌are short ‌and ​clear.

‌Kindred and ​historical ​forms ‌of the ‌name:

- ‌**Japanese** ‌— 火照命 ​(Hoderi-no-mikoto), ‌'Fire-Shining ​Prince'
- **Brother** ​— ​Hoori ‌(Fire-Subduing Prince), ​his ​younger ​brother
- **Parents** ‌— ​Son ​of Ninigi ​and ‌Konohana-Sakuya-hime

​Hoderi keeps ‌its ​restoration ‌plain: plain ​Hepburn. ‌He ‌is a ​minor ​but ​structurally important ​figure ‌in ‌the imperial ​genealogy.

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

domains.body:
**Hoderi** ​is ‌the elder ‌son ​of ​the heavenly ​grandson ​Ninigi ​and the ‌blossom ​princess ​Konohana-Sakuya-hime. ‌His name ​means ‌'Fire-Shining,' ​and he ‌was ​gifted ​with ​the fishhook ​that ​made ‌him master ​of ‌the ​sea. His ‌story ​turns ‌on ​the rivalry ‌with ​his ​younger brother ‌Hoori, ‌a ‌conflict ​that costs ​him ‌his ​birthright and ​sets ‌the ​imperial line ​on ‌a ​new ‌path.[^1]

### Master ​of ​the ​Sea

He ​received ‌the ‌fishhook and ​was ‌meant ​to ​rule the ‌waters.

### ‌Elder ‌Brother

Firstborn ‌of ​Ninigi, ‌but ​destined to ​lose ​precedence ‌to Hoori.

### ​Tragic ​Competitor

​His attempts ‌to ​best ​Hoori ​end in ‌the ​loss ‌of his ​hook ‌and ​his ‌inheritance.

### Ancestral ‌Figure

​Ancestor ​of the ​Hayato, ​a ‌people of ‌southern ​Kyūshū.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Aston, W. G., Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, 1896).
Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

mythology.body:
Hoderi's story in the ​*Kojiki* is a tale of sibling rivalry, the ‌exchange of gifts, and the transfer of sovereignty ‌from the sea to the land. He ​is the elder son, the firstborn of Ninigi, ​destined to be bypassed — and Japan's two ​oldest histories tell his falling-short with different ​temperaments, and the difference is itself instructive.[^1]

### The ​Exchange of Gifts (Kojiki)

When Ninigi's sons grew ‌up, he divided the world's livelihood between ​them: to Hoderi, the elder, he gave the ​fishhook that rules the sea; to Hoori, the ‌younger, the bow and arrow that rule ​the mountains (*Kojiki*, age of the gods). Hoori ‌proposed that they exchange — he would try ​the sea, Hoderi the chase — and ‌Hoderi agreed. But the sea resisted the stranger: ​Hoori fished for days and caught nothing, and ​in a fury he flung the precious ​hook into the waves. Hoderi's response was absolute: ​he would sooner lose a kingdom than his ​hook, and he demanded its return on ‌pain of their brotherhood itself. Cornered, Hoori walked ​into the sea to answer for the ‌loss. The exchange looks innocent but is the ​hinge of the whole cycle: a fisherman's tool, ‌lost and owed, becomes the lever that ​moves sovereignty from elder to younger, from sea ‌to land.[^2]

### Hoori's Triumph (Kojiki)

Beneath the waves ​Hoori found not punishment but fortune: the ‌palace of the sea god Watatsumi, and marriage ​to the god's daughter Toyotama-hime. From the sea's ​depths he sent the lost hook back ‌to land — recovered, in the *Kojiki*'s wry ‌detail, from the throat of a sea bream ‌— bearing a curse that turned against ​its owner: whatever it touched would fail and ​wither. Struck by the curse, Hoderi saw his ‌stores dwindle and his luck collapse, until ​he came barefoot to his younger brother, begging ​terms. Hoori took the submission and the precedence; ‌Hoderi gave him his daughter and his ​allegiance, and the elder line bent to the ​younger. The myth's meaning is economical and severe: ‌legitimacy in the age of the gods ​does not follow birth order but the flow ‌of fortune, and the sea, for all its ​plenty, could not hold the future that ​was gathering on the land.

### Ancestor of the ​Hayato (Genealogy)

The *Kojiki* closes Hoderi's line not ​with extinction but with a dignified office: ‌his descendants are the *Hayato*, a people of ‌southern Kyūshū remembered in early Japanese records as ​warriors and as ritual specialists at the ‌imperial court. Historically the Hayato appear in the ​eighth-century chronicles as a military people whose sons ​served the throne — an echo, scholars ‌have long suspected, of a pre-Yamato population of ‌the south absorbed into the imperial order on ‌terms its own myth explains. The genealogy ‌does double work: it gives the defeated elder ​brother a posterity, and it gives the victorious ‌court a way to honor the people ​it absorbed, as ritualists rather than rebels. In ​Hoderi's house the myth means: the bypassed line ​is not erased but employed — the ‌memory of the elder brother kept on the ​payroll of the younger's descendants.

### The Tide ​Jewels of the Other History (Nihon Shoki)

The ​*Nihon Shoki* (720 CE) tells the same feud ‌with different names and sharper weapons: the ​brothers are called Umisachihiko, Sea-Luck Lad, and Yamasachihiko, ​Mountain-Luck Lad, and the sea god arms the ​younger with the two tide jewels — ‌one that floods, one that ebbs. When the ​elder attacks, the flooding jewel drowns him; when ‌he begs, the ebbing jewel spares him, ​and he swears service to his brother's line, ‌becoming — the genealogy agrees — ancestor of ​the Hayato. The Shoki's variant notes are ‌harsher still: in one alternate account the elder ‌brother does not survive the feud at all. ​Two official histories, two temperaments: the Kojiki ​converts defeat into service, the Shoki leaves the ​sea prince gasping on the tideline. Read together ​they show the early court arguing with ‌itself about what to do with the elder ‌line — absorb it lovingly, or drown it ​and call it law.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Aston, W. G., Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, 1896).
Philippi, Kojiki.

syncretism.body:
Hoderi ​is primarily ‌a genealogical ‌figure, and ​his afterlife ​is interpretive. ​Shinto scholarship ​has long ​read him ‌as the ​mythic signature ​of the ‌sea peoples ​and older ‌lineages of ​southern Japan ‌folded into ​the Yamato ​order ​— his ​'Fire-Shining' name ​suggests a ‌solar brilliance ​eclipsed by ‌the mountain ​brother's steady ‌fire. The ​myth's structure ‌invites comparison ​with other ‌younger-son-victories in ​the imperial ​line (Ninigi ‌himself was ‌passed over ‌for ​rule of ​heaven in ‌favor of ​the narrative's ​landward mission), ‌making Hoderi ​one link ​in a ‌chain where ​sovereignty repeatedly ‌detours around ​seniority. Buddhist ​and Confucian ​readers of ​later centuries ‌found in ‌him a ​lesson ‌in the ​submission of ​fortune to ‌virtue; modern ‌folklorists find ‌an ethnographic ‌memory. He ​absorbed no ‌foreign cult ​— the ​traffic ran ​the other ‌way, his ​story naturalizing ​an absorbed ​people.[^1]

Kindred ‌figures ​in the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index include ‌[[hoori|Hoori]] (elder ​and younger ‌fire brothers), ​[[aseratu|Ašeratu]] (sea ‌/ water), ​[[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]] (sea ‌/ water), ‌[[benzaiten|Benzaiten]] (sea ​/ water), ​[[brigid|Brigid]] (fire ​/ forge ​/ craft), ‌and [[ea|Ēa]] ‌(sea / ​water).

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

cultural-legacy.body: Hoderi ​is ‌little known ‌outside ​scholarly ​and ​ritual contexts, ​but ​his ‌story ​underlies one ​of ‌the ​key ‌narratives ​of Japanese ‌origins: ​the ​transfer ​of legitimacy ​from ​sea ‌to ​land, from ‌elder ​to ‌younger, ​and the ‌inclusion ​of ‌older ​peoples within ​the ‌imperial ‌frame. ‌His ​name survives ​in ‌Kojiki ​retellings, ​in schoolbook ‌summaries ​of ​the ‌age of ​the ‌gods, ​and ​in the ​quiet ​pride ‌of ‌communities in ​southern ‌Kyūshū ​whose ​traditions ‌remember the ‌Hayato. ‌For ‌modern ​readers he ‌is ​the ​necessary ​counterweight to ‌the ​imperial ​success ​story — ‌the ​elder ​brother ​whose loss ‌makes ​the ‌victory ​legible, ‌and whose ​descendants' ‌service ‌reminds ​us that ​Japanese ​identity ​was ‌assembled, not ‌simply ​inherited.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

archaeology.body: Hoderi ​has ‌no ‌independent archaeological ​attestation ​— ​no ​shrine, ​image, or ‌inscription ​names ​him ‌— ​and ‌his importance ​is ‌textual ​and ​genealogical, ​preserved in ​the ​Kojiki's ‌account ​of ‌the ​imperial lineage ‌and ​in ‌the ​Nihon ‌Shoki's parallel ​version. ​The ‌historical ‌echo ‌of ​his myth ​is ‌the ​documentary ​record ‌of the ​Hayato ​themselves: ‌the ​early ‌chronicles ​(Shoku Nihongi ​and ​its ​predecessors) ‌register ‌Hayato delegations, ​military ‌service, ​and ​ritual ‌office ‌at court ‌from ‌the ​eighth ‌century, ​and southern ​Kyūshū ​place ‌names ​and ​burial ​remains attest ‌the ​ancient ​populations ​the ‌genealogy claims ​as ‌his ​children. ‌The ​'evidence' ‌for Hoderi ‌is ​thus ​a ​people ​remembered, not ‌a ‌stone ​inscribed.[^1]

meditation.body: Hoderi ​is the ‌one ‌who ​was passed ​over. ​Every national ​mythology ​crowns ‌a winner; ​few ​pause over ‌the ​brother who ‌held ​the ‌older claim. ​His ​story asks ​us ​to ​notice the ‌elder ​— the ‌sea, ​the ‌firstborn, the ​rival ‌who does ​not ‌win ​— and ​to ‌see how ‌myths ‌of defeat ​are ​woven ‌into national ​identity. ​The Kojiki ‌is ​gentle ​with him: ‌he ​keeps his ‌life, ​his ​daughter marries ​into ​the victor's ‌house, ‌his ​descendants hold ‌honored ​office at ​the ‌court that ‌displaced ‌him. ‌Defeat, properly ​mythologized, ‌becomes service; ​the ​bypassed ​line becomes ‌the ​ritual memory ​that ​legitimizes ‌the bypassing. ​Not ​every ancestor ​becomes ‌emperor; ​some become ‌memory ​— and ‌memory, ​as the ‌court ‌understood, ​can be ​a ​more durable ​inheritance ‌than ‌the throne ​itself.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
Japan's two earliest chronicles, the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE), record Hoderi in mythic narratives of cosmogony and imperial descent. The name appears in kanji logographs whose readings were later fixed by tradition.

The restoration Hoderi preserves the romanized scholarly form derived from those classical sources.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

shinto-sources.body:
Shinto ritual texts, shrine records, and norito prayers preserve the cultic identity of Hoderi. The kami is honored at shrines associated with fire, and festival calendars perpetuate the name.

The Unicode form Hoderi gives that ongoing tradition a precise digital address.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese Buddhist literature and art sometimes assimilate Hoderi into Buddhist cosmology, mapping kami onto dharmic protectors and bodhisattvas. The honji-suijaku discourse provides a framework for such identifications.

The restored name Hoderi appears in both Shinto and Buddhist contexts in the PuniCodex archive.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Hoderi and Hoori cycle; Philippi, Donald L., Kojiki, Princeton University Press, 1969).
